title: Microplastics react with water to make reactive oxygen molecules (Columbia/Berkeley, Nature)

caption:
The plastic in your water may not be sitting there quietly.

A team from Columbia University and UC Berkeley found that microplastics react with the water around them. The reaction produces reactive oxygen molecules, including hydroxyl radicals. They were reported in the journal Nature on November 20, 2026.

Here is why it happens. Many plastics repel water. Hydroxide ions in the thin layer of water next to the plastic lose electrons more easily there, and that turns them into hydroxyl radicals.

Smaller pieces have more surface, so breaking plastic down creates more places to react. Lead author Naixin Qian points out that reactive oxygen molecules are textbook examples of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue.

The same Columbia lab reported in 2024 that a liter of bottled water held about 240,000 detectable plastic fragments, mostly nanoplastics.

The catch: this does not prove the process causes any specific disease in people. The experiments were done in the lab and in simulations, not in living bodies. Earlier studies have linked micro and nanoplastics to heart and brain problems, but those are associations.

So the new question is how much of this happens inside us.

Source: Columbia University via ScienceDaily; Nature
